Unlike existing databases that focus on complex, multi-step reasoning and complex argumentation, ATOMIC selects instances where the relationship between the argument and the conclusion can be linked by a simple causal connection, making it ideal for models that learn through simple if-then patterns. ATOMIC comprises various categories of text-based scenarios that exhibit this characteristic and includes a comprehensive set of sentences that can be used to assess models' ability to perform this type of reasoning. Additionally, we present a novel evaluation protocol that combines the ATOMIC database with a set of specially designed multi-step reasoning tasks drawn from various sources, including the ArgBan dataset. This protocol involves determining whether a model can perform a specific reasoning task by also establishing that it can perform the set of preceding if-then tasks linked to that particular reason. Our results indicate that while current state-of-the-art models excel at individual if-then patterns, they often fail to excel at multi-step reasoning tasks when evaluated using the proposed protocol. Moreover, the evaluation protocol demonstrates that a model's performance on the ATOMIC database does not guarantee the same level of performance on diverse text-based reasoning tasks. Furthermore, the evaluation protocol reveals significant differences in the types of premises that various models are able to work with when given a particular conclusion, indicating a need for more research in the area of text-based reasoning. Additionally, the evaluation protocol introduces a new form of error analysis centered on the concept of a "reasoning trajectory," which is the sequence of connections that a model uses to link the argument to the conclusion. This approach to error analysis highlights a limitation of current evaluation methods that focus solely on the final conclusion, by showing that a model may accurately produce the desired conclusion but fail to do so when its reasoning trajectory is altered, even if the change is minimal. This finding underscores the importance of assessing the underlying connections used by a model when evaluating its ability to perform if-then reasoning. In the conclusion, we emphasize that the database and evaluation protocol presented provide a crucial framework for creating models that excel at multi-step reasoning and that the concept of a reasoning trajectory offers a valuable framework for further research in this area. Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage for sensitive groups, such as pregnant women and young individuals requiring frequent imaging, due to compromised image quality from lower doses or shortened scan times. Deep-learning models have made significant advancements in enhancing PET images by translating low-quality PET scans with associated MRI data to higher-quality PET images, particularly with significantly reduced doses. Nonetheless, such deep learning approaches have primarily focused on utilizing training datasets similar to their test data, neglecting performance evaluation for new acquisitions outside of their distribution. We developed a novel neural network framework that incorporates the physics underlying the PET imaging process and estimates output uncertainty to address these limitations. This new uncertainty-aware neural network framework can utilize low-dose PET scans and accompanying MRI data to generate high-quality PET images at standard doses, thus enhancing robustness when processing out-of-distribution data, such as various forms of OOD PET-MRI acquisitions. Experimental results confirm the advantages of this model in enhancing PET images both quantitatively and qualitatively in various settings. Notably, our methodology demonstrates superior performance when dealing with previously unseen variations in MRI data configurations, such as different acquisition settings and anatomical coverage, for which traditional approaches fail to operate effectively. Furthermore, this framework exhibits comparable performance to state-of-the-art deep learning models when processing in-distribution data but leverages a significantly larger dataset, thereby enabling robust training with more diverse and realistic data, such as extended datasets combining various forms of low-dose and normal-dose PET scans. Additionally, this study explores the challenges associated with data restrictions and explicit data augmentation techniques were employed to ensure robustness with respect to retention of residual out-of-training data information. The implementation of this uncertainty-aware neural network framework led to enhanced PET image reconstruction at lower doses, with a notable average gain of 2.3 in PSNR values, when tested with out-of-distribution data, resulting in the potential for safer, lower-dose PET scans during pregnancy. The developed framework's effectiveness in enhancing real-world PET images under various dose conditions also underscores its potential as a safe and more realistic enhancement tool for available, restricted training datasets. This paper delves into the details of beam dynamics to provide a generalized expression for the beam breakup threshold, taking into account the effects of filling design, machine period, and the 90-degree phase shift caused by the interaction between opposing beams. It highlights the significance of carefully selecting a machine period that is a multiple of the filling period to minimize the impact of filling design on the beam breakup threshold. This paper is particularly useful for the review of recent discussions on the electron beam transport line of the future Higgs factory, although the concepts presented can be applied broadly across energy recovery linac designs. 
  As the threshold equation shows, the beam breakup threshold is essentially determined by the cut-off frequency of the cavity and the distance between the particle trajectory and the central path in the x-direction. However, when considering a filled particle bunch, the situation becomes more complex as the particle's position is shifted in the x-direction following the distribution of the charge bunch. Consequently, the beam breakup threshold will vary depending on the charge distribution within the bunch. 
  To standardize the threshold expression, we introduce a new parameter, the equivalent radius (r_eq), which represents the distance between the particle trajectory and the central path when integrating the charge within a spherical volume. This parameter serves as the filling design dependency factor and is defined by the integral of the x-direction particle position multiplied by the charge distribution, taken over the entire bunch. 
  By incorporating r_eq into the original threshold equation, we obtain a simplified and more intuitive expression for the beam breakup threshold, which now highlights the effects of filling design and machine period on the threshold. It indicates that the best approach to minimizing the impact of filling design is to select a machine period that is a multiple of the filling period, although this may not entirely eliminate the influence of filling design.

Human assessments of both natural and controlled settings reveal that a well-trained Dungeon Master exceeds a baseline in both how easily the players are drawn into the role and the overall coherence of the conversations that follow. Moreover, we explore the role of a theory-of-mind component in comparison to a more straightforward approach that prioritizes conversation guidance. The implications of our work are explored within the broader context of controlled role-playing games as both a testing ground and a method for evaluating the effectiveness of a learning system. Academic researchers who read extensive literature likely pose many questions to themselves in order to plan and execute their research, but unfortunately, they don't always document these questions due to a lack of useful tools. Although question-answering tools like QA systems can provide some insight, they are typically limited to simple queries. In contrast, more complex queries often demanded by sophisticated AI systems require more detailed information and contextual understanding, which is usually derived from dense, implicit, and nuanced knowledge present in academic papers. In order to support the development of next-generation QA systems that can handle such complex queries, we've conducted a survey to gather a diverse range of questions that are relevant to these topics and include links to the underlying research papers. Our dataset of 1000 pairs of questions and answers is unique in its focus on questions that are driven by a desire for knowledge rather than answers that can be verified, which differentiates it from existing datasets like QA-distill, SAM, and NaturalQA. Furthermore, our evaluation results show that models trained on this dataset perform better on a variety of challenging tasks such as zero-shot dataset extension, few-shot query answering, and out-of-domain evaluation when compared to models trained on the existing datasets. Additionally, we observed that models trained on this dataset also exhibit better performance on natural language understanding tasks like SAT and ACL-ARC but similar performance on text classification tasks like TREC. Our dataset, which comprises of 1000 pairs of questions and answers, can be accessed via this link https://www.dropbox.com/s/link?dl=0 and is also hosted on Hugging Face's Dataset platform. Our research indicates that there is a significant amount of useful information that can be extracted from literature reviews, which is often presented in a structured and unstructured manner, and future studies should focus on creating datasets of annotated entities, relationships and concepts that can be extracted from academic papers. Furthermore, we believe that creating such a dataset of knowledge-seeking questions and answers can provide valuable insights and serve as a stepping stone for the development of more advanced models that can handle complex tasks such as reasoning, inference and argumentation on top of massive amounts of scientific knowledge. Additionally, we also contend that such a dataset can facilitate the creation of more effective tools for searching, navigating and exploring the vast amounts of scientific literature contained within academic papers, which in turn can accelerate the pace of scientific progress. Lastly, we also contend that creating such a dataset of knowledge-seeking questions and answers can also serve as a platform for crowdsourcing the development of more sophisticated models

We examine the unique properties of a Majorana fermion, specifically its behavior as a fermionic particle and antiparticle. This analysis yields advanced statistical formulas for linear Majorana fermions. Employing these, we investigate how the conventional anti-symmetry of fermions is compromised in this case. This results in the formation of an asymmetrical Wigner distribution and a quasi-classical Poisson distribution. Furthermore, we investigate how the non-conservation of charge affects the linear Majorana fermion. This leads to the creation of a charge-asymmetric Planck constant and a new, linearly dependent energy-momentum relationship. Consequently, we propose that a linear Majorana fermion could potentially serve as the foundation for a consistent, quasi-classical statistical model. This model may offer a unified explanation for both particle and antiparticle behavior, providing a solution to the consistent continuous spontaneous localization model's particle-antiparticle problem. Moreover, we show that a linear Majorana fermion can provide a link between quantum mechanics and general relativity. Finally, we examine the implications of a linear Majorana fermion for the consistent CSL model in relation to the Mott problem. This analysis reveals that a linear Majorana fermion can facilitate a consistent, quasi-classical description of system dynamics, thus providing a viable solution to the Mott problem. Additionally, we outline the parameters required for a linear Majorana fermion to be compatible with the CSL model and the Mott problem. This includes a charge-asymmetric Planck constant of approximately $2.04\times 10^{-18}$ eV s, a mean free time of around $1.75\times 10^{-21}$ s, and a minimum charge of approximately $2.04\times 10^{-24}$ eV. This research demonstrates that a linear Majorana fermion can offer a consistent, quasi-classical description of system dynamics, providing a viable solution to the Mott problem and further solidifying the model's potential to resolve the particle-antiparticle problem in the CSL theory. This advancement may also give rise to a new understanding of the CSL process, prompting experimental verification of the proposed charge-asymmetric Planck constant, mean free time, and minimum charge. Moreover, a linear Majorana fermion presents an intriguing opportunity for the investigation of quantum systems in the presence of a linear Majorana mean free path. This could give rise to a new area of research centered on the study of quantum systems with a linear mean free path, potentially revealing novel aspects of quantum mechanics

Our investigation focuses on a scenario where two incoming atoms, one of which is coherent and the other is in a superposition, interact with each other and a third particle via a laser field. This leads to the formation of a molecule and an outgoing atom. Our study reveals that the system exhibits a vast array of connected properties, including wave packet dynamics, bound and free fragment correlations, and temporal evolution of interference patterns. Notably, our analysis also highlights the potential for achieving highly entangled states of both atoms and molecules. Furthermore, we find that the system's response to a laser field induces a crossover from three-body recombination to binding, mediated by the phase of an initial coherent atom state. This phase control enables the creation of molecule-atom pairs in either an entangled state or a separable state, depending on the laser parameters. Additionally, we demonstrate that applying a laser pulse that shifts the phase by 180 degrees allows for the transformation of a coherent atom state into an atom-molecule entangled state. This phase control also enables the creation of molecule-molecule pairs in an entangled state. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the optimal production of an entangled atom-molecule pair occurs under a certain laser intensity condition, which, interestingly, is independent of the initial coherent atom state's size. Conversely, the size of the outgoing coherent atom state directly correlates with the probability of this optimal condition, indicating that this optimal intensity represents a critical threshold. Lastly, we demonstrate that implementing a laser pulse with a specific phase and duration can achieve an entangled atom-molecule state with a high probability, even under sub-wavelength distances. This involves a diatomic gas with a scattering length that is half that of a rubidium-87 gas. A brain tumor affects every age group and has the highest mortality rate.  MRI technology is commonly used for tumor detection and diagnosis by radiologists, who must accurately identify the tumor type and area for proper treatment planning.  However, interpreting MRI scans can be challenging and time-consuming for radiologists.  Building on advances in computer-aided diagnosis powered by deep learning, this study presents a multi-task attention directed network (MAG-Net) that efficiently uses MRI images to classify and segment brain tumors in coronal, axial, and sagittal views.  The model is trained on a comprehensive set of MRI images labeled as benign or malignant and characterized by histological type, before achieving exceptional performance on both classification and segmentation tasks according to metrics including dice coefficient, precision, recall, and accuracy.  Notably, MAG-Net demonstrates a unique ability to handle tumors showing both circular and irregular shapes, while also highlighting key areas for further improvement in radiology reports.  The model's code is available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/chethan-bhat/MAG-Net, providing a practical application for computer vision researchers and potential clinical collaborators.  The study also presents a large-scale dataset compiled from multiple sources, comprising over 500,000 pixel-level annotations on over 4000 MRI slices, available for download from https://github.com/chethan-bhat/MCI-BraTS-Dataset and as a part of the MS COCO dataset, thereby making significant contributions to the field of medical computer vision.  The model's ease of implementation and minimal number of model parameters make it an attractive solution for real-world brain tumor diagnosis applications requiring both classification and segmentation.  The study's findings validate the effectiveness of attention-based deep learning models in accurately diagnosing and treating brain tumors with low mortality rates, providing key insights for data to be used in such applications.  The study's easy-to-implement approach providing high-quality output following the attention-based deep learning trend, may prove valuable to future researchers facing similar challenges in the transfer learning, medical computer vision, and natural language processing domains.  The study's difficult initial setup and extensive annotation process serve as a caution for future large-scale dataset compilation efforts, while its large-scale dataset compilation and challenging tumor classification task may prove useful as a future research benchmark, especially given the relatively low mortality rate achieved, the difficulties encountered, and the relatively simple model used with only 18 layers. Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for various applications such as managing flood risks. Current methods can be cumbersome and hindered by the extensive computational requirements, especially for complex networks like CNNs. Traditionally, river hydraulic engineers employ the Saint-Venant equations, although numerical solutions can be time-consuming and limit real-time predictions in data-driven models. In this research, we introduce a novel, rapid shallow water equations solver based on CNNs, which provides accurate flow velocity predictions and eliminates the need for systematic meshing. This innovative method is straightforward to implement and effectively simplifies the Saint-Venant solution. We demonstrate the efficacy of this deep learning-based approach by applying it to river flow velocity prediction in both ideal and real-world scenarios. The results show that this method outperforms traditional numerical solutions while providing comparable performance to the gold-standard method. Furthermore, we explore the benefits of incorporating additional inputs such as river cross-sectional geometry and water depth, which significantly improves the model's performance in complex scenarios. Causal learning represents a significant shift in machine learning, emphasizing the creation of models that accurately capture cause-and-effect relationships in data. Despite significant progress in various domains, several key challenges remain largely unsolved. A prominent hurdle lies in establishing a clear, widely accepted framework for evaluating a model's causal validity. This issue is compounded by the prevalent practice of evaluating models solely on their predictive performance, which often fails to scrutinize their underlying assumptions. As a result, models may inadvertently incorporate superficial patterns that mask a lack of genuine understanding. This problem is particularly pronounced in high-stakes applications, where the reliance on unverified assumptions can have severe consequences. This article will outline a rigorous framework for assessing a model's causal grasp, comprising five essential criteria that collectively form the "CAUSAL" framework. This framework demands that a model display the following attributes: its predictions must be consistent across different observations, the information it extracts from data must be precise, its predictions of the outcome variable are best served by incorporating the input variables, its predictions of the input variables are most accurately made when the outcome variable is considered, and the relationships it identifies are robust in multiple contexts. This framework is adaptable to various types of data and models; its purpose is to provide a comprehensive, all-encompassing standard for a model's causal validity. This article will also explore the application of this framework to a subset of cutting-edge machine learning models, testing their ability to meet the CAUSAL criteria. Deep neural network-based classifiers have a common issue, however - they often provide predictions that seem excessively certain but do not reflect the true likelihood of classification accuracy. This limitation is attributed to the inherent closed-world nature of traditional softmax formulation. As deep learning classifiers operate in an open-world setting, encompassing all possible unseen outcomes, their predictions can inadvertently extend beyond their training data labels. In one-dimensional quasiperiodic structures, certain types of wave propagation exhibit a sudden shift from localization to non-localization at specific, irreducible system sizes. Our study shows that in one-dimensional photonic quasicrystals, this phenomenon is reproducible and linked to a more general mechanism. We demonstrate that in a quasiperiodic arrangement, some discrete lattice sizes can facilitate the non-localization of waves, and that this rule applies universally to various wave types. As a result, some of these discrete sizes become 'delocalization centers', and when the quasiperiodic arrangement is expanded to include them, a shift from localization to non-localization occurs. This rule holds true for any quasiperiodic configuration and can lead to the creation of delocalized states within a finite area. Furthermore, our study shows that in one-dimensional systems, a 'delocalization republic' emerges where multiple delocalization centers can be found, and that the distribution of these centers follows a specific, universal pattern. This phenomenon provides a foundation for the exploration of non-localized states within two- and three-dimensional quasiperiodic structures. Our research also introduces the concept of 'atomic orbitals' in the atomic picture of quasiperiodic systems, and a related 'electron cloud' in solid-state and judicial physics. Finally, some implications of these findings for the construction of electronic quasiperiodic Hamiltonians and the development of applications for wave propagation and scattering are discussed. Our study sets the stage for an in-depth analysis of the interplay between localization and non-localization in photonic and electronic quasiperiodic systems. Additionally, we outline an approach for the numerical simulation of quasiperiodic systems using atomic orbitals and a corresponding 'electron cloud' representation. Our results demonstrate that in one-dimensional photonic quasiperiodic systems, the atomic orbitals of the Dirac comb filter can serve as a universal filter set. We also demonstrate that the critical shift from localization to non-localization in one-dimensional photonic quasiperiodic systems can be explained by considering the universal properties of the atomic orbitals in the atomic picture of quasiperiodic systems. Distributed systems with a shared memory require efficient and effective algorithms to handle failures and maintain data consistency. This paper focuses on the "fence" synchronization primitive, specifically exploring two variants: self-downgrade and self-invalidating. Unlike traditional fence primitives, these variants permit a failed processor to continue executing code, albeit with restricted access to memory. We examine two scenarios: one with n processors, where one processor fails, and another with n/2 processors, where any processor may fail. We provide algorithms to repair fences in the former case and demonstrate that a majority consensus algorithm is necessary for the latter. Additionally, we analyze how our repair algorithms interact with software that relies on the self-downgrade or self-invalidating fence, using two software examples. We also investigate how our repair algorithms perform under various failure scenarios and find that the majority consensus algorithm falls short in the n/2 processor scenario, whereas a combination of majority consensus and a "repair fence" primitive is still insufficient in cases where multiple processors fail independently. Furthermore, we demonstrate that even this combination cannot guarantee efficient repair in certain scenarios. Consequently, we propose a new "3-valued fence" variant, which enables more effective repair in distributed systems. This new variant facilitates the integration of failed processors using a combination of self-downgrade and self-invalidating fences. We analyze two scenarios with n processors, where any processor may fail, and demonstrate that a failed processor can be efficiently repaired using this new variant. Lastly, we discuss potential applications and future directions for the 3-valued fence. This new primitive may be implemented as a hardware component, such as a memory controller or a transactional memory system, or as a software tool using techniques like software transactional memory or atomic sections. This 3-valued fence has the potential to be used in various hardware and software systems, including multithreaded systems, hardware acceleration for software instructions, and virtual machines. Originally proven by Freiman in 1962, his famous 3k-4 theorem essentially posits that if A and B each contain no more than four elements, then A and the sumset of B approximately share many similarities with A plus B approximately. Over the years, researchers such as Gyarak, Shao, Kostarev, Cilleruelo and others have all contributed to various generalizations and proofs of this theorem. Here, the authors present a new corollary that generalizes the theorem for sets of sizes three times any power of two up to (but not including) four times two raised to any positive integer number of powers. This new rule applies under the constraint that A and B, when reduced to their smallest form, have sizes at least one and three respectively. Furthermore, this new rule provides a more efficient sum of sets approximation compared to previously found methods. The authors achieve this new generalization by leveraging a new application of a previous Freiman's 2k-2 theorem proof method and a previously unreported extension of the polynomial method. Additionally, this new generalization results in implications for other problems such as the sum of squares problem and the Erdos sumset problem. Finally, this new generalization also sets the stage for the proof of a much more extensive generalization of Freiman's 3k-4 theorem.

The quality of visual relationship detection (VRD) data is crucial for training models to achieve high accuracy. Unfortunately, certain inaccuracies, particularly in the annotation of subjects, significantly impede the performance of VRD models. In response to the widespread issue of incorrect annotations, many researchers have implemented techniques such as iterative refining and enhanced models, but these methods often fail to address the root cause of the problem and may even introduce additional flaws. In contrast, our proposed framework, Refine-Remove-Rename (RRR), directly targets the elimination of erroneous positives by refining and removing incorrect subject annotations and then renaming the remaining relationships. Experimental results show that RRR yields superior outcomes when compared to the state-of-the-art methods and significantly reduces the number of inaccuracies found in the dataset. Moreover, our analysis of the dataset following the removal of erroneous relationships reveals that it exhibits better properties and facilitates easier training. Furthermore, we discover that certain categories are more prone to errors and, under an extended iterative refinement process, we observe that the accuracy of certain relationships may regressing in the later refinement stages due to the presence of underlying flaws. In line with our findings, we emphasize the importance of incorporating robust refinement techniques that address the fundamental issues with the dataset, and we advocate for the use of more robust refinement techniques under repeated refinement iterations. This report outlines the development of a novel Content Addressable Parallel Processor, built with a Field Programmable Gate Array. Although content-addressable memories have been successfully implemented on FPGAs, our design takes it a step further by incorporating a built-in parallel search function and input data filtering, making it an exceptional tool for optimizing database query performance.

In recent years, big data analysis has experienced rapid growth, but processing large amounts of information remains a significant challenge. One of the most effective techniques is the use of content-addressable memories, a technological advancement that allows for the direct retrieval of information linked to a specific input, circumventing the need for iterative scanning.

However, traditional content-addressable memories suffer from a crucial flaw - they only permit a single reader to function at a time, severely limiting their potential for processing multiple concurrent queries. This problem has sparked the idea for a new type of content-addressable memory that can handle multiple parallel searches, a concept we call a Content Addressable Parallel (CAP) store.

To bring this innovative idea to life, we designed a Content Addressable Parallel Processor (CAPP) using a Field Programmable Gate Array. At the heart of the CAPP lies a large array of content-addressable memory modules, each comprising of a search unit and a filter module. When a write operation is initiated, the corresponding memory cell is updated with the input data and linked to the input content.

During a read operation, the input data is used to trigger a parallel search across all memory cells with the same content, and only the cells whose filtered output matches the input data will generate the correct output, thereby eliminating the need for iterative scanning. This breakthrough design paves the way for the creation of large-scale content-addressable databases that can efficiently handle multiple concurrent queries.

We constructed a working prototype of the CAPP using a Xilinx Virtex-7, and successfully demonstrated its capability to handle up to 64 concurrent search operations on a 256-kbit memory array. Our results show that the CAPP can perform a 64-way parallel search in approximately 12.5 microseconds, a remarkable achievement that surpasses the performance of even the most advanced modern databases. This, along with our design's low power consumption and high scalability, make the CAPP an ideal choice for developing low-latency, multi-core databases that can efficiently handle a high volume of concurrent queries. Furthermore, the CAPP has the potential to be applied in a wide range of fields, including artificial neural networks, genetic algorithms, and cyberspace security systems.

Initially, researchers approximated the UTZ coefficients with a temperature-independent effective lagrangian approach, but this assumption may not hold at high temperatures. By integrating the UTZ model with the effective lagrangian approach and Lattice QCD, we can determine the appropriate temperature range for the UTZ coefficients. Furthermore, we re-analyze the UTZ parameter space using the Monte Carlo Markov Chain (MCMC) method to account for the uncertainties associated with the UTZ coefficients and their temperature dependencies. As a result, we find that the UTZ flavor model can successfully reproduce the observed quark and lepton mass spectra and mixing angles within a specific parameter range. Nonetheless, we discover that the UTZ model faces a challenge in satisfying the neutrino oscillation data while maintaining the 0.01 eV^4 bound on the cosmological effective neutron-neutron interaction strength. Consequently, we find that the UTZ model can only accommodate a right-handed Majorana nucleus mass scale of around 10^12 GeV^2. The revised UTZ flavor model encompasses a more comprehensive and complex parameter space, offering various signature patterns for the search of UTZ-related new physics at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). Therefore, it is vital for both future research and the current development of neural networks to focus on understanding their computations, performance, and behavior. This survey delves into methods for comprehending neural networks through visualization and explanation, highlighting various techniques' strengths and weaknesses, and groups them into three categories: feature importance, visualization of local computations, and visualization of the network itself. It concludes by presenting both ongoing research and potential future directions for the field. In addition, the survey includes an overview of the techniques that address stability issues in training neural networks, the emergence of interpretable neural networks as a distinct research area, and the common applications and performance metrics used to evaluate a network's understanding. Finally, it discusses the significance of understanding neural networks across various domains and fields, and the resulting future research directions and opportunities. Those involved include developing more effective and efficient methods for understanding neural networks, integrating explanations into their training, and addressing the unique challenges posed by new types of neural networks. Furthermore, it also highlights the importance of advancing the field through the development of novel applications and rigorous evaluation methods. Those methods include but are not limited to new visualization and explanation techniques for multi-agent systems, and robust methods for evaluating the understanding of neural networks in different domains. Those domain include but are not limited to computer vision, text analysis, and audio processing, and machine learning, and the underlying mathematics of neural networks. Those mathematics include but are not limited to nonconvex optimization, large-scale linear algebra, and manifold learning. Those domains and mathematics provide both new research opportunities and challenges for those working on the understanding of neural networks. Those opportunities and challenges arise from the unique properties of different types of data and signals, such as images, text, and audio, and the distinct computational properties of different types of neural networks, such as those with different types of weights, such as integer weights, and those with different topological structures, such as recurrent neural networks, and those with different types of connectivity, such as fully connected and convolutional neural networks. The rapid dissemination of news on social media has created a significant challenge to detecting false news, as false news can spread quickly, surpassing the rate at which they are identified and refuted. While machine learning algorithms have made significant progress in this area, their effectiveness is often limited to specific platforms and datasets. Moreover, they often require extensive training data, a significant drawback in this area. To address these challenges, we propose a novel framework, termed MEFN-MNP, that can efficiently detect emergent false news on any platform using minimal adaptation. This framework leverages the meta-learning capabilities of neural process networks to effectively utilize small amounts of training data, combining this with the ability to incorporate diverse information sources, including tweets, Wikipedia articles, and fact-checking websites. By allowing the creation of a new false news meta-process using a single fact-checking sample, our framework can accurately classify unseen data points, including tweets and article titles, that are derived from the same underlying distribution. Our results demonstrate that MEFN-MNP outperforms existing models, including those that have lower accuracy on other datasets, achieving a macro F1 score of 0.813 on the recent Challenging Test Dataset, while also showing that our framework's performance continues to improve over time. This approach, with its efficient, adaptable, and high-performance characteristics, provides a promising solution for the ongoing false news detection challenge. This work also highlights the potential applications and effectiveness of neural process networks in detecting false news, while also highlighting potential issues with fact-checking datasets, such as the presence of false negatives, which may result in the inclusion of false news articles in training data. This limitation highlights the need for more rigorous fact-checking procedures, particularly for critical issues like false news detection. This work is a direct outcome of the dialogue established at the 2020 NLP Challenge Forum, focused on constructing a joint false news detection system, and the implemented solution, with all associated code released on GitHub, serving as a model for other competing teams. This code, combined with the provided dataset and fact-checking guidelines, is now available for any user, enabling the creation of a unified false news detection system. The speed at which astronomical research advances is directly influenced by the efficiency of its underlying technological framework. While automated, remote software systems, often referred to as 'astrobots,' have the potential to significantly boost productivity in data processing operations, simply deploying them without thorough testing is not sufficient. This paper reports the findings of a rigorous evaluation conducted on the latest version of the SDSS data processing pipeline, designed to detect the presence of solar system objects, using a cohort of astrobots comprised of six distinct configurations. Our experiments revealed that all astrobots were fully coordinated in all tests, a crucial prerequisite for their effective deployment. This achievement confirms the feasibility of using these systems for independent deployments. Moreover, our results demonstrate the capacity of astrobots to achieve marked improvements in processing speeds and reduced turnaround times. For the data set size encountered in the SDSS, a significant improvement in processing time was observed, with some astrobots processing the data in half the time required by the benchmark implementation. This improvement is particularly evident in the small data sets, where the fastest astrobot processed the data at a rate eight times faster than the benchmark. This experiment has implications beyond solar system object searches, as it sets a high standard for which future data processing pipelines will be measured against. Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on numerous language tasks. However, despite their significant potential, understanding how to effectively integrate these models into systems of structured knowledge continues to pose a significant challenge. Our proposed framework, SKILL, addresses this issue head-on. SKILL enables the incorporation of structured knowledge into transformer-based language models through a novel form of input that combines both text and knowledge graph inputs and appropriate prompt-based triggers. By doing so, SKILL enables a single model to efficiently process both unstructured language and structured knowledge graph inputs, thereby successfully demonstrating its effectiveness on a diverse range of multi-step reasoning tasks. Our results show that SKILL's knowledge-injected models outperform both baseline models using only language inputs and models relying on separate query and reasoning components. On the MATHIOI dataset, a knowledge graph-based benchmark requiring multiple steps of reasoning, SKILL's models achieve nearly 10% higher scores than the current leader, earning them the top spot. Moreover, our research highlights the critical role that prompt triggers play in enabling these models to execute complex reasoning tasks efficiently and accurately. By integrating both language and knowledge graph inputs, these prompt triggers serve as the missing link to address the issue of structural knowledge, a challenge that previous studies have failed to fully grasp. Our results also raise important questions about the need to develop novel evaluation protocols tailored to assess the ability of models to perform complex, multi-step reasoning tasks. In the context of the MATHIOI dataset, such a protocol would focus on the timely execution of ordered actions rather than mere accuracy. In the evaluation context of the CMC 2023 dataset, comprising natural language explanations, our research highlights the significance of leveraging knowledge graphs that mirror the structure of these explanations to enhance their coherence and natural flow. Lastly, our work highlights the potential for knowledge-triggers to enhance the performance of models operating in limited-data settings, a critical aspect of real-world applications. In the knowledge-triggers domain, our research identifies the challenge of scaling the number of supported actions, a issue that previous studies have addressed in isolation without a unified theory. Our results show that the integration of structured knowledge, via knowledge triggers, enables the development of more efficient and effective multi-step reasoning systems. System performance improves significantly when the knowledge triggers are optimized for each individual action within the reasoning pipeline. Furthermore, our research demonstrates the potential of a novel form of knowledge-triggers known as recursive triggers, a innovation that raises fundamental questions about the need for distinct start and end tokens for the query and reasoning components. Our team utilized the KOOLS-IFU on Seimei Telescope for integral field unit (IFU) observations of 9 ultra/luminous infrared galaxies located close to our own (z < 0.04) and participating in the GOALS survey. These targets span a broad spectrum of merger phases, from early stages to advanced. With the IFU data we collected, we successfully isolated several distinct emission lines including hydrogen beta, oxygen III at wavelength 5007, hydrogen alpha, double-ionized nitrogen at wavelengths 6549, 6583, and sulfur II at wavelengths 6717, 6731. Our analysis with spectral resolutions ranging between 1500 to 2000 allowed us to derive spatially resolved ionized gas maps as small as 200-700 parsecs, as well as active galactic nucleus (AGN) diagnostics within 3-11 kiloparsecs of our targets. Our data show a correlation between active galactic nuclei and the outflow of gas as oxygen III, a trend that is (1) most prevalent in the centers of galaxies and (2) stronger at later stages of merger. For example, during late stages of merger we measured an outflow 1.5 times as powerful as during early stages of merger. These observations imply a relationship between the interaction of galaxy mergers and the outflow of gas that is likely induced by active supermassive black holes. Our team plans to investigate further the connection between the accumulation of gas during mergers and the resulting active galactic nuclei activity that follows. Optimistically, our observations may provide a new explanation for the sudden onset of active galactic nuclei observed over the history of our universe. Ultimately, our study highlights the capabilities of the KOOLS-IFU on Seimei Telescope for exploring the physical properties of galaxies throughout the history of our universe. With the telescope's high spectral and spatial resolutions, we believe it has great potential in contributing to a wide range of galaxy evolution studies. During the between-period, known as the Phase-1 period, limited data were collected with the upgraded detector, featuring a novel digital readout system and distinct pixel chip designs, including the CMS Phase-1 Pixel Pilot Blades developed in Japan. These pilot blades, featuring 1D pixel arrays, served as the forerunners to the current 3D pixel sensors. Given their novel architecture and the absence of relevant reference data, a thorough approach was necessary to establish their calibration and tracking capabilities. Recent advances in open-domain dialogue models have achieved significant breakthroughs, however most current approaches focus solely on conversational role, failing to consider the impact of user specified roles. In reality, many conversations require particular roles from the participants, without assigned roles, natural language understanding (NLU) components would need to explicitly extract roles from user input, complicating system implementation. Furthermore, certain roles may lead to divergent or undesirable conversations, thus it is essential to incorporate role information into the dialogue system. In this paper we propose a unified framework that incorporates both user roles and aims to tackle NLU challenges. The framework consists of a role-aware pre-trained language model for NLU tasks and a series of neural dialogue manager modules corresponding to distinct roles. Results show the proposed framework outperforms a baseline model by over 20% in relevance and nearly 10% in naturalness according to user evaluations. The model also demonstrates efficiency in implicit role extraction and superiority to non-role-aware models in engaging conversations. The framework's effectiveness is further validated by significant reductions in intended action errors and improved diversity in conversations. Tensor network representations of physical states and their time-dependent dynamics require a delicate balance between capturing the system's dynamics and maintaining a precise understanding of its local properties. While the use of time-dependent tensor networks has been extensively studied, its implementation can result in a loss of locality precision in the description of the state. This phenomenon limits the effectiveness of time-dependent tensor networks in two key areas: the description of thermal states and the measurement process. In thermal equilibrium, states are often characterized by a few local observables, whose autocorrelation values can be derived from the density matrix. Similarly, the measurement process involves local interactions with the system. To address these challenges, this paper introduces two new tensor network templates that accurately describe thermal states and time-dependent evolution. These templates include a thermally averaged matrix product state template and a time-dependent matrix product state template with a precise local description, whose use is demonstrated through examples of the Ohmian model and the Lieb-Liniger model. Results show that these new templates yield consistent predictions with existing methods for the Ohmian model but offer a precise local description. In addition, these new templates facilitate the incorporation of physical properties, such as the chemical potential and temperature, in a more manageable way than standard time-dependent tensor networks. Furthermore, this approach allows for the integration of time-dependent and thermal tensor networks, demonstrating that time-dependent evolution can be accurately captured using thermal tensor networks with a precise local description. This framework addresses the fundamental issue of locality precision in the description of thermal states and time-dependent evolution, potentially enabling the practical application of tensor networks in quantum many-body systems. This new approach is also shown to result in stable and efficient contraction methods, underscoring the robustness of this framework. In conclusion, this study offers a groundbreaking contribution to the field of tensor network simulations, resolving a critical limitation and paving the way for its broad adoption in the study of quantum many-body systems. In particular, it presents a solution to a critical challenge facing the community, namely the accurate description of thermal states and time-dependent evolution using tensor networks. This achievement is expected to facilitate the exploration of quantum phenomena in systems of which a wide range has a non-trivial equilibrium or dynamical behavior. In the words of the authors, this study resolves an "existential issue" for tensor network simulations, revealing the possibility of creating simulations that accurately capture the system's local properties. This result is a significant improvement over previous standard time-dependent tensor networks, which fail to deliver a precise local description. This study is a landmark moment for tensor networks

Imitation learning has emerged as a highly effective means of training efficient and accurate models, notably for complex tasks like robotics demonstrations and video sequences that contain subtle labels. Despite its promise, the method is hindered by a critical limitation: it relies on an abundant and high-quality dataset of expert demonstrations. In reality, such data is often scarce, poorly collected, or contaminated with subpar performance from novice or amateur sources. The addition of sterile neutrinos to the Standard Model is often accomplished via a right-handed neutrino sector with a direct, neutrino mass term. However, this approach has issues with scale and naturalness. In contrast, neutrino mass generation via the electroweak symmetry breaking and a high bare mass for the right-handed neutrinos addresses these concerns effectively. In this context, the degree of mixing between the left-handed and the right-handed left-handed neutrinos must be extremely minuscule for the model to be viable. As a result of this extremely constrained parameter space, the numerous degrees of freedom typically introduced by sterile neutrinos are eliminated, and thus the name "Shadow Matter". Despite these constraints, such a model can still accommodate explanations for the observed ark matter density, as well as phenomena associated with long-lived majorons, and even certain oscillation patterns associated with electron (anti)neutrino flavors. However, it cannot explain flavor oscillations in mu and tau flavors. The model predicts extremely short decay lengths for all hadronically interacting sterile neutrinos, making their detection via such interactions extremely challenging. Nevertheless, it may still be possible to detect oscillations in neutrino telescopes like IceCube, particularly for a certain combination of neutrino and neutrino flavors. Between October 2019 and April 2020, the LAMOST performed a unique observational study using four $K$2 plates. This study, which involved low- and medium-resolution spectroscopic surveys, gathered a significant amount of data. The low-resolution spectroscopic survey yielded around 767,000 spectra after 25 nights of 46.6 hours of exposures and a low signal-to-noise ratio higher than 10 for about 70% of its spectra. The medium-resolution spectroscopic survey took 177 exposures and around 49.1 hours over 27 nights to collect around 478,000 spectra. The data showed a low signal-to-noise ratio higher than 10 for about 50% of its spectra. To estimate the stellar parameters and radial velocities, the LAMOST research team utilized several different methods such as LASP, DD-Payne, and SLAM. These estimations demonstrated good agreement and were consistent with those of the APOGEE study. By analyzing the $Gaia$ DR2 data, the LAMOST research team corrected for radial velocity zero points on a per exposure basis, showing good alignment with the APOGEE study. To estimate stellar masses, the LAMOST research team utilized stellar parameters and multi-band magnitudes in combination with distances and extinction values. Ultimately, the LAMOST research team constructed a binary catalog of around 2,700 candidates through the analysis of their light curves, radial velocity fitting, the extraction of binarity parameters from medium-resolution spectra, and cross-referencing it with the $Gaia$ EDR3 binary catalog. This study is expected to significantly impact scientific research in several areas such as binary systems, stellar activity, and stellar pulsations. The LAMOST research team completed binary catalog cross-referencing with the $Gaia$ EDR3 binary catalog and incorporated their findings into the construction of the LAMOST catalog. This study is expected to lay the groundwork for future studies using time-domain surveys on new and upgraded astronomical facilities. The LAMOST research team strongly believes that time-domain spectroscopic surveys on large telescopes will be pivotal in solving some of the most complex scientific research problems in the coming decades. To facilitate easy access to the data, the LAMOST research team constructed an easy-to-use website at http://www.lamost.org/time-domain/. The LAMOST catalog is set to be released in the fourth quarter of 2021 in the VizieR catalog database under the catalog identifier III/384.

Thanks to advancements in computer vision and machine learning, analyzing facial expressions is now a well-established technique for emotion recognition across various settings. However, analyzing speech emotions presents a greater challenge due to the complex nature of speech as a signal, the lack of clear visual cues, and the necessity to effectively integrate audio features with emotion labels. A key obstacle in this domain is the limited availability of large-scale, high-quality annotation data necessary for training models using deep learning methods. This issue is addressed by our proposed framework, which utilizes transfer learning and minimal annotation data to train a deep reinforcement learning-based speech emotion recognition model. The framework is tested on the Affective Dimensions (AffD) dataset and demonstrates superior performance when adapted to real-world applications. Results show that it outperforms a similar model trained exclusively with abundant annotation data, and that it is capable of delivering 11% to 20% improved accuracy on specific adaptation tasks. The code for this project is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghaith3/speech-emotion-Adaptation. This research provides a key contribution to the field of speech emotion recognition, and the method it presents may also be applicable to other domains involving transfer learning and minimal annotation data. Furthermore, our findings suggest that deep reinforcement learning can be a highly effective approach for building models from limited data in the real-world setting. This research is a precursor to additional studies aimed at further exploring the capabilities and limitations of this method. In particular, future studies will examine additional transfer learning scenarios and the potential of this method for building models from even more limited annotation data. We present an investigation of Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ (BFTO-4L), a four-layer Aurivillius compound, under the influence of high pressure on its magnetic properties.  Our X-ray diffraction data does not exhibit a phase transition under pressure but lattice compression is uniform.  Despite compression, the Fe$^{3+}$ 2p-X-ray photoemission spectrum remains the same and shows no change in spin state.  However, our results from nuclear forward scattering indicate a significant increase in the hyperfine field at the $^{119}$Sn nucleus when replaced for Ti and under applied pressure.  Our calculations using the GGA+U method show that this enhancement arises due to the increased hybridization between the Ti 3p and O 2p orbitals under pressure, leading to a rise in the spin polarization of Ti 3d electrons.  This increased spin polarization results in a greater magnetic field at the $^{119}$Sn nucleus under pressure.  Our data also reveal an enhancement in the magnetic moment of the Fe$^{3+}$ ions with the increase in pressure, although our experiments under higher pressure show a reversal in this trend.  Our findings suggest that BFTO-4L holds promise as a suitable reference material for in-situ nuclear resonance measurements under various conditions.  Furthermore, this study highlights the potential of BFTO-4L to exhibit complex electronic properties under pressure, making it an interesting compound for further investigation. In 1930, mathematician K. Menger developed an interest in the abstract concept of angle function, which he then generalized for use in metric and semi-metric spaces. Building upon this foundation, he presented two specific problems concerning the embedding of spaces with angle functions into the structure of Euclidean spaces. Over time, researchers focused on these problems, though only in the context of certain specific types of metric spaces. This article aims to enhance the definition of angle function to accommodate spaces with the property of betweenness, which it deems a more fundamental framework. Within this revised framework, the article provides solutions to Menger's initially posed problems. Furthermore, it identifies additional theorems and corollaries that arise from this revised definition, providing insights into the relationship between spaces with angle functions and the structure of Euclidean spaces. This article also explores the concept of preserving the order of points when embedding spaces with angle functions into the structure of Euclidean spaces, ultimately establishing the sufficient condition for this preservation. This condition is then applied to derive the sufficient and necessary criteria for the embeddability of spaces with angle functions into the structure of Euclidean spaces, which is met when the associated operator defined by the angle function is both positive definite and compact. The Forsage cryptocurrency scheme, considered one of the largest pyramid scams in history, has been the subject of analysis by these researchers who have been studying smart-contract scams since 2020. Working with cybersecurity experts and law enforcement, they have gained a deeper understanding of how Forsage's developers successfully evaded detection for over a year. This paper will outline the technical details used in the implementation of the Forsage scheme, as well as the methods employed in its security breach assessment. This analysis demonstrates that while Forsage's developers utilized various anti-reversing techniques typical of cybercrime tools, these measures were ultimately circumvented through a combination of contract functionality discovery and user participation. This case study provides valuable insights for both security professionals and researchers, offering a demonstration of the type of security vulnerabilities that smart-contract scams and pyramid schemes can pose, and the importance of collaborating with both industries and law enforcement in the development of secure and regulated blockchain applications. This analysis may also contribute to the development of more effective methods for detecting and preventing similar types of smart-contract-based fraud schemes. The catalog of the VVV survey's globular cluster candidates in the bulge of the galaxy is examined using infrared color-magnitude diagrams from the VVV survey. The analysis includes the use of diagrams such as the Ks-[L']0.21V band color-magnitude diagram, the radial velocity distribution of the bulge, and the stellar population models of the bulge to identify and characterize the clusters. The findings of the study are presented in a list showing the coordinates, estimated distance, metal content, radial velocity, and population type of each cluster. A total of 19 clusters were analyzed and their characteristics were often consistent with established globular clusters within the bulge; however, the iron content of three clusters could not be determined due to a lack of relevant data. The results show that multiple globular cluster candidates identified in the bulge of the galaxy have fundamental characteristics such as estimated age, metal content, and radial velocity that align with those of the galaxy's ancient globular clusters located outside the bulge. The presence of these features supports the theory that the galaxy's bulge underwent a collapse, a process similar to the formation of the galaxy's halo, and that the time of the collapse in the galaxy's early stages was nearly simultaneous. In this context, we explore certain classes of holographic tensor networks, which can efficiently simulate various systems using a minimal number of entanglement units. These networks have two key properties: they comply with the holographic principle, which states that the information within a given region can be represented at the boundary with the same accuracy, and they maintain a specific level of invariance. For systems where invariance can be achieved through simple transformations, such as universal invariance, the required number of entanglement units can potentially be significantly reduced. However, many physical systems exhibit more complex patterns of invariance and require a comprehensive analysis. We introduce the concept of hyper-invariant MERA, a more complex variation of the holographic tensor network that can adapt to these scenarios. Using a system of spinless fermions on a lattice as an example, we demonstrate how a hyper-invariant MERA can be constructed and show that its entanglement structure conforms to a power-law pattern, a common feature observed in many physical systems. Furthermore, we discuss the implications of this construction on the scalability of hyper-invariant MERA and the related holographic code, suggesting that while these systems can exhibit power-law behavior, there may be a critical temperature threshold where the code's fidelity begins to degrade significantly. The hyper-invariant MERA framework provides a new pathway for developing holographic quantum computing models that can emulate the complex phenomena observed in physical systems. The example construction presented here highlights the potential of this framework to create scalable, fault-tolerant holographic codes, a crucial step towards the development of practical holographic computing applications. The discussion on the scalability of these systems, the associated decoding errors, and the impact of temperature on code fidelity presents a compelling case for further exploration of this framework in the context of quantum computing, potentially leading to the creation of scalable, stable, and efficient holographic code constructions. Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to severe distortions when transferred to new contexts. This study reveals that existing smoothing techniques for point clouds often fail to preserve the underlying geometric structure, resulting in the distortion of model predictions. To address this issue, a new algorithm called Transformation-Unique Smoothing is proposed, which maintains the structural integrity of point clouds through a unique smoothing property. The method surpasses the current state-of-the-art smooth models in multiple evaluation metrics and successfully applies smoothing to a range of challenging scenarios, including data augmentation, missing data interpolation, and model transfer. We're investigating medium access techniques in Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave (FMCW) radar networks with all radar units utilizing identical settings, such as sweep duration and frequency characteristics. We're developing and evaluating ALOHA and CSMA protocols to minimize the impact of narrowband interference, introducing a new metric to gauge performance based on network throughput. In the case of ALOHA, we analyze the probabilities of interference and system efficiency under different system parameters. We observe that FMCW network behavior diverges from typical wireless communication patterns. In some scenarios, increased packet transmission can decrease interference probabilities. We introduce a clear channel assessment process, known as medium sensing, for CSMA, also defining metrics to gauge its effectiveness. In our analysis of CSMA, radar units transmit data after confirming an empty transmission path. We examine CSMA's medium sensing success rate, interference probabilities, and system efficiency under different system parameters. Unlike standard communication networks, the optimal strategy in some scenarios may involve the highest feasible attempt rates for maximizing throughput. Extensive simulations are conducted to validate our analytical findings and compare the efficiency of slotted ALOHA and CSMA. In our analysis, CSMA consistently outperforms ALOHA across all practical use cases. Notably, ALOHA's performance is significantly better when the average number of radar units is lower than the ideal range for CSMA. ALOHA's throughput can be over ten times higher in certain scenarios. Through these comparisons, we demonstrate the importance of tailored communication protocols in FMCW radar networks. A hybrid approach, a combination of ALOHA and CSMA, may further enhance throughput but would greatly increase the complexity of the system. Therefore, we recommend adopting time-slit CSMA, a simpler method with CSMA, to achieve better performance. In this variant, CSMA is applied across different time slots rather than across all units within a single slot. This approach results in better performance than standard CSMA but still significantly better than ALOHA, with only a marginal decrease in throughput. Ultimately, time-slit CSMA offers a more substantial increase in throughput than the hybrid approach but with minimal increase in attempt rates. Temporal knowledge graph completion has emerged as a leading approach for
inferring temporal knowledge graph relationships. Unlike their static counterparts,
temporal knowledge graphs feature relationship timing information, capturing transient
knowledge that expires over time and must be addressed. Current methods typically
combine techniques from temporal modeling and knowledge graph embedding, but their
high dimensionality can result in inefficient representation and difficulty in handling
limited and noisy data common to smaller knowledge graphs. Existing approaches often
yield representations that are both high-dimensional and graph-specific, hindering their
extensibility to other graph types. To address these limitations, we propose a novel
approach that leverages low-rank and model-agnostic representations for time-aware
representation learning. This approach extracts time-dependent and time-independent
components from entity and relation representations, ensuring that these combinations
are efficient (i.e., low-dimensional) and versatile (i.e., model-agnostic). We design
a new temporal factorization module that segregates time-dependent and time-independent
components from temporal and relational factors. We further explore the benefits of
our approach by comparing it to state-of-the-art methods on six diverse knowledge
graphs, demonstrating that it excels in precision and efficiency while offering the
ability to adapt to other graph types, such as ontologies and taxonomic graphs. Our
approach achieves superior results than existing state-of-the-art methods on the TKG-Benchmark
v2.0 and also finds applications in real-world scenarios, like temporal and relational
node classification, by enhancing the performance of models like Graph Attention Networks.

We introduce a novel prompt-based architecture called HyperPrompt, which utilizes a separate set of prompts to guide a task-conditioned transformer to perform multiple tasks simultaneously. In contrast to standard prompt-based models, which use the same prompts for both input and parameter updates, HyperPrompt employs unconnected prompts as input, and a separate set of prompts to modulate the task-specific attention and feedforward layers. This paper investigates the regularity of solutions to a non-autonomous obstacle problem, formulated as follows: given a bounded, Lipschitz function $f$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, we seek to find a function $u$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ that minimizes the functional $\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(x,u(D_t x))dx$ among all functions $u$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ satisfying the compliance condition $u\geq v$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, where $v$ is a given lower bound. We extend and refine prior results by Ambrosio and Dal Maso, addressing cases where the growth of $f$ with respect to $u$ satisfies sub-quadratic conditions more finely, specifically exponential, polynomial, and power growth conditions. Additionally, we establish results for sets $D_t$ with non-smooth boundaries and derive new outcomes for set $D_t$ with irregular boundaries. This essay explores the development of the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory from 1921 to 1957, during the tenure of director Pieter Johannes van Rhijn, who succeeded the lab's founder, Jacobus Cornelius Kapteyn. When van Rhijn took over, the lab was working to implement Kapteyn's Selected Areas Plan. However, van Rhijn's contributions were marred by his lack of exploration into the broader implications of his findings, potentially stemming from limited creativity or vision. Throughout nearly his entire directorate, van Rhijn struggled to secure additional funding due to severe challenges including the 1930s Depression, the Second World War and its aftermath, his personal health issues during the 1940s, the lab's distant location, and a governmentally favored infrastructure in Leiden. Lastly, the circumstances that led to Adriaan Blaauw accepting the position of director in 1957, setting in motion the revitalization of the lab, are analyzed in the latter half of this study. Van Rhijn's life and career are briefly outlined in the introductory chapter, while the following chapters examine the Kapteyn Lab's research activities, its place within the international astronomical community, and the challenges the lab faced during Van Rhijn's leadership. The unique combination of decentralization, immutability, and pseudonymity behind cryptocurrencies has made them extremely popular with illicit actors, who take advantage of them to execute malicious transactions efficiently. As a result, currency trail analysis, a fundamental skill in security and forensic research, has become vastly more complicated due to the high level of transaction anonymity afforded by cryptocurrencies. In an effort to better grasp this new reality, our research focuses on enhancing currency trail analysis by leveraging advanced machine learning techniques to detect patterns in illicit actors' transaction behavior and develop a more comprehensive understanding of their financial pathways. By combining natural language processing and graph-based approaches, our work aims to provide a more nuanced view of the underlying mechanisms that illicit actors use to move currency, and reveals the presence of distinct trails associated with different types of malicious activities, as well as the importance of considering the underlying blockchain topology when analyzing currency trails. Furthermore, our research demonstrates the effectiveness of a proposed algorithm, which is capable of predicting transaction behavior and identifying new members of specific malicious groups based on updates to the blockchain and user feedback. By successfully identifying and predicting key features of currency trails, our work paves the way for more effective counter-measures, such as targeted alerts and blocking of suspicious transactions, and lays the foundation for further research into the complex interplay between malicious actors, transaction behavior, and currency trails in a blockchain-based ecosystem. By answering some of the basic questions surrounding currency trails, our work also highlights a number of intriguing research questions that arise in the context of blockchain-based networks, and the potential benefits of applying complex systems theory to the study of cryptocurrency and security. In the end, our work demonstrates the potential value of a hybrid approach that combines graph theory, machine learning, and human expertise for analyzing currency trails and preventing malicious activities in a blockchain-based ecosystem. Additionally, our research was conducted using the Bitcoin blockchain, but the same principles can be applied to other cryptocurrency-based blockchains. Our work is the first of its kind to examine currency trails in a blockchain-based ecosystem, and the code used for the experiments and results presented in this paper is publicly available at https://github.com/aleixcat/understanding-currency-trails. This code is part of the Cryptoforensics Toolkit, a collection of general-purpose algorithms for analyzing currency trails and predicting transaction behavior in a blockchain-based ecosystem. This paper was presented at the 2019 IEEE Conference on Technologies for Sustainable Development, ICSDE 2019. This research was supported by the Government of Catalonia and the European Union's ERDF

This work utilizes the concepts from Generalized Degrees of Freedom (GDoF) analyses and extremal network theory to investigate the benefits derived from utilizing optimal power control as opposed to a binary variant in a general K-user interference network. Through examination of various examples, including those at the extremal ends, we demonstrate that the obtained GDoF results with optimal power control, as reported by Liu, Li, and Li (2013), differ from the binary power control GDoF by a $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ amount, where $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ indicates a function that scales with $\sqrt{K}$. Moreover, our analysis provides a lower and upper bound for this $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ benefit in terms of GDoF, and proposes a name, Extremal GDoF Benefit (EGB), to quantify this advantage. EGB is found to be directly related to the maximum number of independent paths between interferers and the receiver in question, denoted as $R$. With this definition, we establish that any network containing at least one path with four or more nodes (i.e., $R \geq 4$) will achieve a sub-optimal binary power control performance, whereas networks with isolated triangles (grapes) or more extensive graph structures (granite) will still exhibit superior binary power control results in terms of EGB. The term EGB is subject to the constraint that total power is constrained by the binary choice, indicating an interesting analogy to the recently introduced term super-far field in extremal network theory. Finally, we explore applications of this EGB framework to evaluate variously configured K-user interference networks. For example, consideration is given to exclusive access, shared access with cross-ambient interference constraints, and CDO channels. These analyses provide a framework for extending existing knowledge on power control in a broad range of interference networks. A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain deformations both its solid and liquid components pose. At their core, both substances defy rigid body predictions according to Newton's laws. Current robotic locomotion approaches rely heavily on force feedback and learned strategies but tend to focus on solid surfaces or highly controlled environments. In contrast, this project simulates a single leg on top of a semi-liquid base with dimensions much larger than the leg itself. Unlike previous models featuring heart-shaped cavities, the newer model incorporates a more comprehensive analysis that includes a broader range of frequencies. This simulation reveals the emergence of a new high-frequency mode and demonstrates how a larger footprint reduces the impact on the surrounding fluid. Effective information reading is a crucial skill for numerous applications, including text summarization and text classification. Despite being an inherently complex task due to the presence of negations, contractions, and other linguistic nuances, current systems are able to perform well on available datasets that test basic fact retrieval. To evaluate their ability to grapple with the intricacies of natural language, there is a need for expanded datasets that include more sophisticated reasoning elements. In this paper, we introduce CONDAQA, a 5480-question strong base dataset that demands a deeper understanding of the relationships between statements, including those that involve negations, contractions, and other linguistic nuances. Our dataset and rigorous evaluation results indicate that substantial improvements over existing systems are possible with the use of negation-aware models, achieving nearly 72% overall accuracy with models that are specifically designed to perform well on such tasks. These models, trained with methods that emphasize contrastive learning, demonstrate a notable 22% increase in performance when compared to existing state-of-the-art models. The source code and data for CONDAQA are publicly available at https://github.com/ghrua/CONDAQA. The used prefix-based approach is similar to that employed in the LowDataQA benchmark, and we adopt the same evaluation protocol as stated in Section 3 of the LowDataQA paper. The primary variation lies in the type of reasoning that each dataset demands, with LowDataQA focusing on relationships between statements that do not involve negations and CONDAQA targeting those that do.
