Planets orbiting stars of types K and G pose unique challenges for astronomers, as their distant worlds must be analyzed through spectral patterns, often influenced by water vapor and other gases in their atmospheres.  As a result, the composition and properties of these exoplanets are not well understood, especially those surrounding K stars, due to the limited nature of current observations. Each label was assigned by multiple experts in conjunction with a comprehensive characterization of the contents of each slide, which can be downloaded in part or in its entirety from one URL. Our initial effort at UniToPatho focuses on classifying normal, hyperplastic, serrated neoplastic, adenomatous, and malignant tissues using whole-slide images. Although expert characterization surpasses their ability to analyze individual 1024x1024 tiles, our current state-of-the-art model, which combines a patch-based classification system and a neural network, achieves 0.309 in mean average precision when evaluating entire slides. Moreover, our implementation of a characterizing neural network that accounts for each 1024x1024 tile's context yields 0.237, closing the gap between experts and the model. UniToPatho's diversity and extensive size make it an ideal target for developing and evaluating cutting-edge histology analysis algorithms. Furthermore, our experience reinforcing models with a patch-based system, guided neural networks, and a form of expert-labeled pseudo-positive mining, collectively known as UniToPatho's Patch-Based Neural Network, has the potential to influence the evolution of deep learning methods in the field of digital pathology. UniToPatho's Patch-Based Neural Network is comprised of over 120 Gb of data, including over 3,400 expert-labeled whole-slide images, along with over 17,000 annotated H&P slides, which can be downloaded from one URL. A novel numerical strategy has been introduced for solving time-harmonic acoustic scattering issues, primarily centered around analyzing the impact of smoothly varying material inhomogeneities on plane waves. This method's efficiency is optimal for high-frequency scenarios and is adaptable across any given frequency $\omega$. The approach operates within a time-domain framework, consisting of three main components: generating a suitable incoming plane wave with compact propagation direction, solving the time-domain scattering problem, and ultimately deriving the time-harmonic solution via Fourier transformation. Crucial to this approach is a dynamic front-tracking mesh refinement technique which minimizes the required number of finite elements needed to achieve a desired level of accuracy by limiting the computation to a compact region surrounding the incoming wave's support. This strategy results in an element-independent order of convergence of $O(\tau+\omega^{-1}h)$ in the time-domain setting and $O(\omega^{-1}h)$ in the time-harmonic setting, where $\tau$ represents the time step size and $h$ the element size. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through numerous numerical experiments conducted under various intense external sources, including incident plane waves and point sources. These results showcase the approach's superiority over traditional finite element methods for solving high-frequency time-harmonic scattering problems. The implementation of this strategy leads to computationally efficient solutions even for large-scale problems, as evident from the scalar versions of several challenging benchmark problems analyzed. One such problem involves the scattering phenomenon within a large, irregularly-shaped material inhomogeneity for both time-harmonic and time-domain settings. This strategy's adaptability and accuracy make it highly suitable for addressing future technological challenges involving scattering problems, particularly those with smoothly varying material inhomogeneities. The time-harmonic implementation of this approach is also applicable to volumetric boundary conditions via the J-L map. This is first demonstrated through a new acoustic uniqueness result derived for time-harmonic problems, which in turn has implications for time-domain uniqueness results. This approach is currently being further optimized for further potential applications involving nonlinear scattering problems. The optimized strategy's potential applications and future research directions are also discussed in the accompanying discussion paper. Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in medical imaging has been explored - using realistic modifications of chest X-rays to correct existing flaws. Current GAN-based models excel at producing realistic medical images but struggle with accurately depicting anatomical details, particularly when it comes to modifying existing images. Recent advancements in image-to-image translation have shown improved performance in this area, but these models often sacrifice realism for accuracy. Building upon the strengths of both GANs and image-to-image translation models, our model combines a conditional Wasserstein GAN with a reverse architecture, while incorporating the guidance of anatomical features. By validating the approach with an lung cancer dataset, the results demonstrate that the model not only produces more realistic images but also accurately depicts key anatomical features. Furthermore, the model's performance in editing real chest X-rays demonstrates substantial improvement over a baseline model.
